deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page is a table, Sept. 4–28, comparing computed and observed places of a planet. Two values identify it as Saturn. log r ≈ 0.98 gives r ≈ 9.56 AU. The retrograde motion is about 4'/day near the September opposition. The year fraction 1817,74 (= late Sept. 1817) fixes the date. The last row of that table is Sept. 28: Calc 358°0'15,68", Obs 358°0'5,10", difference +10,58". This page is the full worked computation of that Sept. 28 place from the solar and Saturnian tables (the Saturn tables are probably Bouvard's, in centesimal degrees). The 358° quantity turns out to be the right ascension.

(1) Time of observation, top left.
- t_obs = 11h24m33.4s Göttingen mean time.
- Subtract the light time 1h10m23.6s (= 4223.6 s; it is derived at the bottom right of the page, as I show below): 10h14m9.8s.
- Subtract the Göttingen–Paris longitude difference 30m26s: 9h43m43.8s Paris mean time, written 9h43.74m (more exactly 43.73m) = 9h.729.
- 9.729/24 = 0.405375. With the half-day shift of the table day count this gives the argument 'Sept. 28,905375'. The 1817,74 beside it is the date as a year fraction.
- The line 'Magl. 28.10.11,15667 = 28.10,18594' is a sexagesimal-to-decimal conversion: 11.15667"/60 = 0.18594'. The quantities following it (= 28,42441; 271,42441; 3,86) I cannot identify with certainty.

(2) Arguments of the Saturn perturbation tables, Roman-numeral row.
- Table arguments II…XVI are given in units of 1/10000 of the circle: 8757, 8687, 7387, 138, …
- Below them are two rows of small numbers. The first appears to be small corrections to the arguments (39, 13, 25, …). The second (32, 54, 109, −8, …) is uncertain; it may be the tabular equations themselves, with partial sums 891, 832, 293, 579.

(3) Heliocentric longitude, in grads, first column.
- Mean motion pieces: 4.11302 + 1.03866 − 0.90221 = 4.24947 g.
- Epoch 392.44331 + 4.24947 + 0.00786 = 396.70064 g.
- Add the sum of the periodic and elliptic equations 0.63411 g, taken from the second column, where table entries Nos. 2–17 (3133 + 24133 + 31895 + … + 17) sum exactly to 63411: 397.33475 g.
- Apply −0.02278: L = 397.31197 g.
- Multiply by 0.9: 357.580773° = 357°34.84638' = 357°34'50.78".
- Apply a small correction −3.81": L = 357°34'46.97".
- In the second column, 99.45546 + 0.00163 = 99.45709 g, very plausibly the perihelion longitude (= 89.51°). Then (400 − 99.45709) + 4.24947 = 304.79238 g is the anomaly-type argument used to enter the tables.
- In the third column, 124.54319 + 0.00073 = 124.54392 g, very plausibly the node (= 112.09°). Two partly illegible numbers follow.

(4) Radius vector.
- 9.49744 + (1319 + 828 + 2791 + 202 + 187 + 31 + 643 + 76 + 5)·10^-5 = 9.55826 AU.
- log r = 0.9803789.

(5) Heliocentric latitude.
- 251741 + 236 + 41 + 6 + 1 = 252025, i.e. 2.52025 g.
- × 0.9 = 2.268225° = 2°16'5.61" (south).
- log cos β = 9.9996596 and log sin β = 8.5974501.
- log(r cos β) = 0.9803789 + 9.9996596 − 10 = 0.9800385 (curtate distance).
- log tan β = 8.5977472 n is written and then struck out.

(6) Earth/Sun.
- 279°48'2.00" + 85°5'6.84" + 3.10" + 14.20" + 0.06" + 14.42" + 35.33" = 4°54'15.95". This is the Earth's heliocentric longitude, i.e. the Sun's longitude + 180°.
- A log column 0.0004542 + 89 + 24 + 502 (×10^-7) = 0.0005157. Probably this is log R with small corrections; uncertain.

(7) Heliocentric to geocentric.
- Commutation E − L = 4°54'15.95" − 357°34'46.97" = 7°19'28.98". Its log cos is 9.9964414.
- The parallactic angle L − λ' = 0°51'13.50" gives λ' = 356°43'33.47".
- [My check:] the series Σ (R/r')^n sin n(E−L)/n reproduces ≈ 3071" ≈ 51'13".
- Ratio of curtate distances: log(r' / ρ') = 0.0476787 (= 8.6454259 − 8.5977472).
- log ρ' = 0.9800385 − 0.0476787 = 0.9323598.
- Geocentric latitude: log tan β' = 8.6454259 n, i.e. β' ≈ −2.53°, from tan β' = tan β · r'/ρ'.

(8) Obliquity.
- 23°27'47.09" + 0.09" + 9.42" (nutation) = 23°27'56.60".
- log cos ε = 9.9625107 and log sin ε = 9.6001016.
- A small sum −0.61 − 0.09 − 0.16 − 0.01 = −0.87" (a further small correction).

(9) Right ascension.
- Formula: tan α = tan λ' cos ε − tan β' sin ε / cos λ'.
- log tan λ' = 8.7574339 n; + log cos ε gives 8.7199446 n.
- The second term is 8.6454259 + 9.6001016 + 0.0007095 = 8.2462370. Here 0.0007095 = −log cos λ'.
- The difference is taken with Gaussian subtraction logarithms (argument 0.1778082): log tan α = 8.5421364 n.
- Result: α = 358°0'15.68". The observation is 358°0'5.10", so C − O = +10.58" (as on p. 206).

(10) Distance and light time.
- log ρ' is recomputed/corrected to 0.9324080. Subtracting log cos β' = 9.9995762 gives log Δ = 0.9328318 (Δ ≈ 8.565 AU).
- log Δ + 2.6928469 (log 493 s, light time for 1 AU) gives 3.6256787, i.e. 4223.6 s = 1h10m23.6s.
- This is exactly the light-time correction subtracted from the observation time in (1). The page is thus a closed loop: compute the place, derive the aberration time, re-reduce the epoch.

The items 4.6250941 → 4.6256098, 9.1050846 → 9.1056003 (each + 0.0005157 = + log R) and 9.5778290 + 49 belong to the same parallax/distance computation. I cannot pin down each factor with certainty.
errors: 9h43m43.8s is written '9.43.74'; strictly 43.8s = 0.73 min, so 9h43.73m. The decimal 9h.729 and 0.405375 d are nevertheless correct.
My recomputation of α from the logs on the page gives ≈358°0'15.2" against Gauss's 15.68". The difference is within the precision of my check, so no clear error.
The figure 9.1050846 does not match log sin(7°19'28.98") = 9.105487 exactly. It is probably a different auxiliary quantity, not an error; unresolved.
Some struck-out entries (8.5977472 n, 0.9800867, 9999518) are abandoned intermediate values, not errors in the final result.

results.what: Reduction of a Göttingen meridian observation time to Paris mean time with light-time (aberration) correction, Δ·493 s.
results.modern_name: Light-time correction / reduction to table meridian

results.what: Heliocentric longitude, radius vector and latitude of Saturn for 1817 Sept 28 from centesimal planetary tables with perturbation arguments II–XVII.
results.modern_name: Planetary ephemeris computation from tables (Bouvard-type Saturn tables)
results.usually_credited_to: Bouvard (Tables of Jupiter and Saturn, 1808/1821), Laplace theory

results.what: Heliocentric → geocentric conversion (annual parallax 51'13.5", geocentric latitude via tan β' = tan β·r'/ρ').
Ecliptic → equatorial: tan α = tan λ cos ε − tan β sin ε / cos λ, evaluated with Gaussian addition/subtraction logarithms; apparent obliquity with nutation.
results.usually_credited_to: classical; Gaussian logarithms credited to Gauss/Leonelli

results.what: Comparison computed vs observed right ascension of Saturn (C−O = +10.58"); this series is published in Gauss Werke VI, p. 428.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine observatory reduction: Saturn's place computed from standard tables and compared with a Göttingen meridian observation, including light time and nutation. The associated table on p. 206 is marked as published in Werke VI 428. There is nothing methodologically new.
